items.title: Ray Drummond interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003
items.q: Bill Mays, the two recordings with Bill I really enjoy, you know just the two of us playing

ctx.x: Would that be on your short list of things you’ve played on that you feel the best about?

Yeah I think so. Yeah. Definitely. I’d have to say that probably “Excursion” is one of the things that — it’s not that I’m most proud of, because for instance like Hank and Billy, that record, I love the music on it, there are certain engineering values that I’m not too terribly excited about but forget their playing, they’re playing is always exemplary but it’s just the project and the way it came about and what happened as a result, I mean when I listened to it, it’s just a marvelous, Bill Mays, the two…

you know you hire people because of their individual voices and you put them together not because you want them to make a sound that you think they should make but because you hear what they do and you want to put them together with the individual voices so that they will interact and make whatever sound comes out of that. And that’s what Miles did. Miles would always do that. Miles was not a person that said I want you to sound like this, I want you to play like this. If anything Miles said, “Uh, you’re not…

items.title: Bill Mays interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 5, 2025
items.q: I’ve played with such a wide variety of bass players who had such different sounds and feels and approaches from Ron Carter to Ron McClure, Red Mitchell to Ray Drummond, Martin Wind to Dean Johnson, Tommy Cecil, Todd Coolman.

ctx.x: It was a great statement. Let’s talk about bass players. The reason I went that direction is because that last little piano excerpt I played you had taken – your left hand became a walking bass. And over the years I’m sure you’ve worked with many bass players, sometimes by choice, sometimes by circumstance. What do you like or not like to get from a bassist?

Well I want them to be in tune, I want them to be just a tiny, tiny bit on top of the beat generally. I want them to be able to play with the bow because I use arco in a lot of my presentations. They need to be good readers some of the time, if it’s a project that requires that and then I’ve played with bass players who weren’t good readers but had tremendous ears. I want them to be supportive and contributive. I want them to be able to just play time and keep it really basic sometimes, and then I want them to…
Well you know we were just talking about the difference from one bassist to the next. And you know what? What don’t you want the bass player to do?
